analysis.investment_thesis: Eris has good operating margins (26%) and strong revenue CAGR (19%), but this growth has been purchased entirely with debt — borrowings exploded from near-zero to Rs 2,389 Cr in just three years, pushing D/E to 0.68, far beyond my absolute limit of 0.5. Most damning: net profit in FY25 (Rs 375 Cr) is barely above FY21 (Rs 355 Cr) despite revenue nearly tripling, which tells me the acquisitions are destroying value, not creating it.
key_strengths: Operating margins of 26.4% and gross margins of 73.9% reflect a genuinely strong branded formulations franchise in chronic therapy
Revenue CAGR of 19.2% over nine years is impressive in absolute terms, demonstrating real market share gains
OCF turned strongly positive in FY25 at Rs 1,065 Cr, suggesting the acquired assets may be starting to generate cash
key_risks: Debt/Equity of 0.68 is a hard red flag — borrowings went from Rs 0 in FY20 to Rs 2,389 Cr in FY25, with finance costs surging to Rs 231 Cr
ROE of 12.9% and ROCE of 12.2% are below my 15% minimum — meaning the capital is not being deployed efficiently
Net profit is stagnant at Rs 355–406 Cr from FY21–FY25 despite massive capital deployment, signalling poor acquisition economics
red_flags: Aggressive debt-funded acquisitions tripling total assets from Rs 2,226 Cr (FY22) to Rs 7,160 Cr (FY25) in three years — this is exactly the behaviour that destroys long-term wealth
P/E at 45.2x is more than double my upper threshold — the market is pricing in a recovery that hasn't materialised in bottom-line profits
Finance costs exploding from Rs 2 Cr in FY21 to Rs 231 Cr in FY25 shows a business that has fundamentally changed its risk profile
analysis.detailed_analysis: Eris built a genuinely good business through FY22 — steady chronic-therapy focus, clean balance sheet, and consistent profits. The decision to aggressively acquire assets in FY23–FY24 (evidenced by investing outflows of -Rs 975 Cr and -Rs 1,828 Cr) has transformed it into a leveraged roll-up that must now service Rs 231 Cr of annual finance costs. Net profit has not grown in four years despite the revenue base nearly tripling — this is the clearest possible signal that acquisition premiums were too high or integration is failing. At 45x P/E with a balance sheet this leveraged, the risk-reward is poor. I built DMart without taking on debt; I would never invest in a business that grows by borrowing what it cannot yet earn.
